lf-num.description: A measured number in prose, tied to the data run that produced it.
lf-num.x-instructions:
Write the value with its unit as the element's text, with `source` naming the feed that measures it. Write that element into the page before calling `leaf data set`, then set `run` to the returned receipt. Add `via` when the source id doesn't say which command or query produced it.

The value stays as you wrote it. Any later write to the source, even of the same value, makes `page check` advise that the number needs another look. Use one source id per measurement.

lf-text-document.description: Text written in the page, or from page data or a widget output, with numbered lines, syntax coloring, and an optional Markdown or HTML preview.
lf-text-document.x-instructions:
Write text that belongs to this version of the page, such as a passage you quote, in the `<pre>`, HTML-escaped (& before < and >), and name where it comes from with `label`. HTML drops a newline right after `<pre>`; every other character is part of the text. For text that changes apart from the page, bind `source` to the page's data source, or `for` to a widget publishing a `document` output, leave out the `<pre>`, and name the file with `label`. Set `preview` to `markdown` or `html` to add Preview and Source tabs over the same text. `language` colors the source, and defaults to the preview's language. An HTML preview is a separate document that inherits no Leaf styles, and comments can't reach inside it, so the user comments on the source. A Markdown preview of text written in the `<pre>` takes its rendered height up to `--lf-bound`, 28rem by default, and its Source tab shows as much of the source as that height holds, with a press for the rest. Other documents, such as bound ones, whose text arrives after the page first paints, scroll inside a box that tall however long the text. To start it collapsed, put it inside `details`.

## Refreshing a source

A Markdown file bound to a source:

```html
<lf-text-document
  id="skill-source"
  source="leaf-skill"
  label="SKILL.md"
  preview="markdown"
></lf-text-document>
```

Set the source to one JSON string. For a whole file:

```bash
jq -Rs . SKILL.md | leaf data set <page> leaf-skill
```

For a selected line range instead:

```bash
sed -n '71,102p' SKILL.md | jq -Rs . | leaf data set <page> leaf-skill
```

Run the pipeline again to refresh the open page. `references/authoring-evidence.md`,
"Source files and media", owns when evidence follows a source and when it keeps a snapshot.

lf-options.description: Alternatives the user can choose individually or as a set to answer a question.
lf-options.x-instructions: Keep shared premises and evidence with the group (lf-ask can frame its question and context), and each alternative's own case and picture inside its lf-option. `multiple` lets the user pick several options as one answer (references/authoring-on-me.md says when). Option cards read down the group, each as wide as the group. `across` on the `lf-options` sets them side by side, which suits a group where what the user compares, each option's picture or the evidence above the list, still reads at a card's share of the row, and the question then fits the window. Keep them reading down where that share would shrink the pictures below the size at which their difference reads. The built-in Another option field takes unlisted answers, so add no catch-all option; `closed` leaves it out where only the listed options can answer, such as a page that draws its own choice, and the user can still say more in a comment. Use `for` only to point at sections or work items that exist apart from the question. A `multiple` group needs the user's Done even when `chosen` is authored. When taking in an answer in a stamped version, write `chosen` on exactly the picked `lf-option` elements you authored. Leave an option the user added out of the markup; the log keeps it. Once you have finished applying the decision, give the group `settled`, which collapses it to the pick while keeping its options and anchors.

lf-option.description: One alternative in a decision: a compact label, or a card showing what choosing it gives the user.
lf-option.x-instructions: Word, label and illustrate the alternatives as `references/authoring-on-me.md` says. Use a direct `<strong>` child for a card's title. Follow it with any consequence the title or labels leave unstated, and put pictures in block HTML, such as `svg.drawing`. Mark the option you advise with `<small class="tag ok">recommended</small>`. Give your reason for the recommendation in prose beside the group, such as the `lf-ask`'s paragraph, so each card states only what choosing it does. Direct text takes inline Markdown. `chosen` records the user's pick. Use `$restated` to withdraw that pick and ask again. A `for` target must stay useful whatever is decided, and does not supply the option's words. `value` names what the option answers wherever a view shows the group's answer, such as a board column (read the `lf-board` instructions for the composition).

lf-code.description: A source-code excerpt with syntax coloring, highlighted lines, and line-anchored remarks.
lf-code.x-instructions: Write the exact code inside pre at column 0, HTML-escaping & before < and >. Set language for source code and omit it for plain transcripts or command output. For excerpts, set lines to the ascending source ranges quoted, such as 1505-1507,1520-1527; hi and lf-note at then use those source numbers. A note addressed to an omitted line captions the elided row.

lf-note.x-instructions: Set at to the line number as the parent numbers it: 1-based by default, or the source number declared in lines.

lf-chart.description: An Observable Plot chart authored with Plot’s API and sized to its place in the page.
lf-chart.x-instructions: Inside a `<pre>`, write a JavaScript expression for the options object you would pass to `Plot.plot`, HTML-escaping & before < and >. `Plot` and `width` are the names in scope, and the data goes inline. The chart requires an `ariaLabel` describing it. Leave `width` and `height` out of the options: read `width` to fit the ticks to the room, and set a height other than the default with `data-height` on the element. Write dates as ISO strings on an explicitly typed time scale, `utc` for days and months, and give moments a time zone, such as 2026-06-01T14:00Z. Use `var(--series-N)` for constant or categorical colors; a continuous color scale needs a Plot scheme. Title the chart in the heading or prose around it rather than with Plot's `title`. The reader sees each point's value by pointing at it, by focusing the chart and stepping with the arrow keys, or by holding a finger on it, on every line, area, bar, cell, dot and rect. The tip names the point by where it stands and then what it measures, a line for each, its label then its value, as in "week 6" over "offline sessions 8,412". To say something else, give the mark a `title` channel, such as `title: (d) => ...` among its options: its first line replaces the place and the rest the value. To show values on only some marks, or on a rule or text, give those marks Plot's `tip` option, and the others show none. The tip says the channels Plot's own tip would, those Plot's `channels` option adds included, and reads Plot's tip options: `format` to word a channel, leave it out or bring back one Plot's tip leaves out, and `pointer`, `maxRadius`, `px` and `py` for what the pointer picks. Leaf draws the tip, so leave out Plot's `tip` mark and `pointer` transforms. When `page check --render` reports overlapping labels, use fewer category ticks, choose them by `width`, or give the axis label more margin. Plot takes a mark's `dx`, `dy` and `textAnchor` as one value for the whole mark, so labels that each need their own offset, such as line ends that meet, each take a mark of their own.

{
  ariaLabel: "Hours to first review by week: backend fell from 31 to 12, frontend from 18 to 11",
  x: {type: "utc", ticks: "monday", label: null},
  y: {grid: true, label: "hours to first review"},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["var(--series-1)", "var(--series-2)"]},
  marks: [

lf-shot.description: A before-and-after pair of screenshots with paired, slider and pixel-difference views, change outlines and scale controls.
lf-shot.x-instructions:
Use it for two versions of an interface. Set `before` and `after` to the paths `leaf page media` prints, and describe the pair in `alt`. `references/authoring-evidence.md` covers capture preparation, laying out captures that vary along more than one axis in a table, and registering media. Put explanation in the prose around the pair, not inside the element. When a decision turns on the change, put the pair inside the option that proposes it, or, for an accept-or-reject decision, with the group, where it shows both answers.

Check the pair as it first appears: Fit
shrinks the captures to the available width and, in Slider and Pixels, to the screen's
height, so a long full-page capture shows small. Choose crops and page space that make
the relevant change readable there, without requiring the reader to zoom first.

Every pair starts in **Slider**, followed by **Pair** and **Pixels** in the shared
header. Before and After label the header, or each frame when stacked. Pair keeps
the captures at the same scale; clicking either image opens its original. Fit places them beside one another or stacks
them, whichever draws them larger, so short wide captures stack and tall narrow ones sit
side by side; stacked frames fit together within the screen or the comparison's height limit. At 100%, both panes stay visible and scrolling either image moves
the other to the same location. This scale uses CSS pixels when capture metadata
supplies the pixel ratio, or bitmap pixels otherwise. The **…** menu offers Fit,
100%, Outline changes, the Changed pixels color key and, for a pair with focus metadata, Full
frame to inspect beyond that region.

In Slider, click or tap the image to alternate between the complete Before and After
frames. Drag the divider for an intermediate comparison, or focus it and use the
arrow keys; Home and End show the complete frames.

**Outline changes** marks changed regions in Pair and Slider, using the accent color
for content that only moved. **Pixels** paints changed pixels amber over the greyed after image, softly for
small changes and more strongly for large ones, so build no difference image of your
own. It locates differences without inferring what was added or removed. These controls belong to the reader; author the pair with `before`,
`after` and `alt`.

The comparison reports identical images, slight changes or changes throughout the
frame. If it reports identical images, or no outline sits where the prose puts the
change, capture a case that shows the change or say that nothing changed. Name subtle
changes in the prose. Where live data changed between captures, say where to look.

The option cards

The chips now sit above the title, so a scanning eye reads cost before prose.

lf-board.description: Cards grouped into columns for scanning work and status, with movement and reordering available.
lf-board.x-instructions: Use a board to show grouped work and status. When the user must make decisions, give them explicit controls or `lf-options` rather than relying on moving cards. When revising, place each card in the column and rank `state` gives it (`$state` defines ranks), unless the revision retracts that move by marking the card, not the board, `restated` (`authoring-revisions.md`, "Honor user state"). ## One answer in its section and on a board For this composition, read the `lf-options` and `lf-option` instructions too. When the user answers proposals beside their cases and also needs every answer in one view to compare or rearrange, keep each answer in its section's `lf-options` and add a board whose cards show those answers, rather than asking twice. Give each option a `value` naming the answer it gives, in words every section shares, and the board one column per value with that `value`, plus one column without a value for proposals not yet answered or answered in the user's own words. Each card's `shows` names its section's group, and the card appears in the column matching that group's selected value: ```html Next Later Keep the rail ``` A drop on the board answers through the group, so the page holds one answer, which Undo and `restated` take back in both views. When a revision writes the user's pick into the group, move the card to that pick's column too. A card that shows an answer keeps the order you wrote it in; where the order within a column is itself the user's call, ask for it as its own question.

lf-column.description: One named board column, including empty columns the user can move a card into.
lf-column.x-instructions: Write a label that names the column on its own. Use tone when landing here carries a status judgment, such as blocked, needing review, or done; otherwise leave it neutral. On a board whose cards show answers, `value` names the answer the column holds, and a column without one holds the answers that name none.

lf-card.description: One board card whose identity and comments survive user moves.
lf-card.x-instructions: Lead with a `<strong>` title and follow with prose. Keep its id stable across moves. Use `$restated` to withdraw the user's moves. `shows` makes the card a view of a decision widget's answer: it stands in the column whose `value` that answer names, and moving it changes the answer (read the `lf-board` instructions for the composition).

lf-tabs.description: Several views shown one at a time: page navigation, a tabbed box, or a queue beside its open item.
lf-tabs.x-instructions: The first `lf-tabs` written directly in `main` owns the page's view history and URL. Give a set `class="layout-flow"` to share the document's space without a frame, as page-layout.md describes; omit it for a boxed tab set. Visual flow does not choose history ownership. Put the page's title and lede before page tabs, and the main current view first. Make each `lf-tab` a self-contained view; history, threads and versions belong to the whole page. When current work no longer needs a view, remove it. Move any context still needed, and any passage an open thread or an unretracted decision is anchored to, into a `details` in the relevant tab. Use `list="side"` for a queue listed beside the item it opens.

lf-draft.description: A block of text the user owns and can rewrite in place, with recorded revision history.
lf-draft.x-instructions:
Write the exact Markdown source as `

` right after it. HTML drops that first newline; every later character, indentation and trailing newlines included, is part of the draft. With `needed`, a draft asks the user for an edit; without it, it is an optional editing surface. Use lf-ask when the request needs its own heading and evidence. For approval of editable wording, read authoring-on-me.md, "Permission". When taking in an answer to a `needed` draft in a stamped version, write the user's exact words as its body, using the `
` form above. Keep the user's exact source on revision (authoring-revisions.md, "Honor user state"); to replace an edited passage on purpose, write the new text and mark the draft `restated` ($restated).
